messages.subject: Re: SEM with random treatment (estimation in one-step of factor model and outcome equation)
parts:
Partly the same problem. The estimated parameter for an endogenous variable is an intercept, not a mean.

But if you center all covariates (across both groups) on the control-group mean, you might get what you want, depending on whether you have missing data and how it is handled.

At this point, we've long stopped talking about lavaan as software. SEMNET is for more general discussions ( https://listserv.ua.edu/cgi-bin/wa?SUBED1=semnet&A=1 ) or a general introduction to SEM, which are plentiful.

On Fri, Apr 16, 2021 at 7:05 AM Ale Dea <aaal...@gmail.com> wrote:
But is it possible to constrain only the mean of the control group (estimating the variance)? How would this be done in the laavan syntax? 

On Friday, April 16, 2021 at 12:57:48 PM UTC+2 mal...@malonequantitative.com wrote:
I don't have an example handy. As I've said, it is not a standard thing to do. The variance of an endogenous variable is not a parameter of the model. Forcing it to a specific value is something you'll have to do the work on.

The usual practices for scaling a latent variable are to either constrain its disturbance variance to 1 or constrain a factor loading to 1. Any introductory material on SEM will cover this.

On Fri, Apr 16, 2021 at 4:02 AM Ale Dea <aaal...@gmail.com> wrote:

Can I ask you what the standard practice to deal with latent factors and experiment would be then? It seems that it is not to create indexes with mean 0 and standard deviation 1 as in kling et al

For the constraints? You'd need to familiarize yourself with path-tracing rules, for which there is lots of material.

I don't recommend this, though. It's a lot of work for a fairly arbitrary goal.

On Wed, Apr 14, 2021 at 3:31 PM Ale Dea <aaal...@gmail.com> wrote:
I see, could you please point me to some references if you have specific one in mind?

On Wednesday, April 14, 2021 at 4:34:41 PM UTC+2 mal...@malonequantitative.com wrote:
You could conceivably do it with some fancy constraints, but it's not an intuitive or common thing to do in a latent-variable context.

On Tue, Apr 13, 2021 at 4:02 PM Ale Dea <aaal...@gmail.com> wrote:
Thanks Pat, what you say makes perfect sense. but I am still a lit bit confused. How can I estimate a regression of a factor on a treatment status and control (e.g. knowledge ~ treat + controls) where the factor has mean 0 and standard deviation 1 in the control group in one-step?

On Tuesday, April 13, 2021 at 8:55:59 PM UTC+2 mal...@malonequantitative.com wrote:
No, it won't work in the same way.

First, "treat" is your grouping variable instead of being a predictor--remember, it's constant within group. The effect of treat is seen in a between-group difference in the intercepts of knowledge.

Second, the variance of an endogenous variable ("knowledge") is not a parameter of the model. So the "1" in "knowledge ~~ c(NA,1)*knowledge" is a disturbance variance, not the variance of knowledge. And there's no assurance that the disturbance variances in the two groups are otherwise comparable once you've added controls. Even if the controls are perfectly balanced by randomization, they may have differential effects by groups (interactions).

Pat

On Tue, Apr 13, 2021 at 2:27 PM Ale Dea <aaal...@gmail.com> wrote:
I see what you mean, I can implement what you suggest and make it analogous to Kling by having the model below. Then the change in the intercepts of knowledge is my treatment effect. But is it possible to twist the code below to have the results in a regression form and include controls? Like adding this line (# knowledge ~ treat + controls), I have tried adding this line but it does not work

knowledge =~ test1 +test2+test3+test4
# Fix mean and stand deviation in control group
knowledge ~ c(NA, 0)*1
knowledge ~~ c(NA,1)*knowledge 
#regression
# knowledge ~ treat + controls
'
# strong invariance
fit3 <- cfa( model, data = fullsample, group = "treat"  , group.equal = c("intercepts", "loadings")) 



On Tuesday, April 13, 2021 at 2:07:54 PM UTC+2 mal...@malonequantitative.com wrote:
Regardless of whether you go the factor score route, then you need a two-group model with measurement invariance, and base the scores on that model, if it fits. If it does not fit, then you need to decide what to do from there.

To make it analogous to the Kling situation, you would constrain the variance and mean of the latent in the control group to 1 and 0 and freely estimate them in the treatment. But the loadings and intercepts need to be equal for the comparison to be meaningful.

On Tue, Apr 13, 2021 at 5:02 AM Ale Dea <aaal...@gmail.com> wrote:
Thank you Carl. The aim of the analysis is to test if the treatment has an effect on the factor score (for example, the knowledge).
You say "If you want to test the effect of the treatment on the factor, then the factor loadings and the intercepts of the measured variables must be set equal across groups." isn't this exactly  what I would do if I estimate the factor model on the control group and then I predict the treated group's factor scores with the model fitted on control group data?


The test of invariance is a good idea, it would be an additional check which my data shall satisfy given the random allocation of the treatment. I was proposing the method above because the final equation I would like to estimate is
knowledge(after treatment)= b*treatment +c*knowledge(before treatment)
where both measures of knowledge before and after the treatment come from a measurement system and I am interested in the coef b. I am not sure if this can be encompassed in a multigroup factor model




On Monday, April 12, 2021 at 9:02:47 PM UTC+2 car...@web.de wrote:
I had overlooked that: It is not necessary to calculate factor scores to make a statement about the mean difference of the latent variable. "Then if I find strong invariance, I predict the factor from the configual invariance and compare the means. On the other hand, if I only have weak invariance, I can only compare the distribution of the latent factors from the configural model in the treatment and control groups, correct?" No, I don't think that's correct. However, I don't understand what exactly you want to do here.


Am 12.04.2021 um 17:21 schrieb Ale Dea:

Thank you Carnold, yes so you are suggesting to do the following:
# configural invariance 
fit1 <- cfa(model, data = fullsample, group = "treat") 
  # weak invariance 
fit2 <- cfa( model, data = fullsample, group = "treat"  , group.equal = "loadings") 
  # strong invariance
fit3 <- cfa( model, data = fullsample, group = "treat"  , group.equal = c("intercepts", "loadings")) 

  # model comparison tests 
lavTestLRT(fit1, fit2, fit3)

Then if I find strong invariance, I predict the factor from the configual invariance and compare the means. On the other hand, if I only have weak invariance, I can only compare the distribution of the latent factors from the configural model in the treatment and control groups, correct? 

Do you mean that the model I propose is misspecified because I am forcing the factor loadings in the control group to be the same as ones in the treatment group to predict the factor scores in the treatment group?  


 

On Monday, April 12, 2021 at 4:35:18 PM UTC+2 car...@web.de wrote:
Well, because otherwise you are comparing apples and oranges and/or - as Pat mentioned - fitting a misspecified model. The difference you mention between the groups should be reflected in the mean difference and not in the factor loadings etc.

I have already named the proposed model. There are not too many variants that fit my description: https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/groups.html

Are you familiar with multi-group models and invariance tests?
Am 12.04.21, 16:20 schrieb Ale Dea <aaal...@gmail.com>:
The reason why I want to do the following is because if I fit a factor model on treatment and control group data, then the factor loadings would also pick up the variation in the responses induced by the treatment. 
On the other other, if I fit the factor model only on the control group data, then I can use it to predict the factor scores for the treatment and control group. (I do not have the problem above and I can use the random assignment to study how the treatment group's factor scores differ from the control group. The key intuition is similar to compute an index a la Kling et al (2007) where they standarize the responses in control and treatment group by subtracting the mean and dividing by standard deviation in the control group (to have an index with mean 0 and standard deviation 1 for the control group) and study how the random assignment affects the index.) 

Dear Carnold, could you please elaborate what model (i.e., multigroup model with invariance test and a mean-difference comparison) you are suggesting? Why do you suggest testing for invariance between control and treatment group if I have a random assignment which should make the treatment and control group different? 

Many thanks

On Monday, April 12, 2021 at 2:42:18 PM UTC+2 car...@web.de wrote:

I'm not entirely sure what you're up to. Model 2 would basically be a MIMIC model. If you want to look at the effect of the treatment on the factor: What's wrong with a multigroup model with invariance test and a mean-difference comparison?
Am 12.04.21, 14:09 schrieb Ale Dea <aaal...@gmail.com>:
Dear all,

I am using lavaan to explore an impact evaluation of a randomized control trial where the outcome variable is a latent factor and the treatment is randomly assigned. 

I would like to estimate the latent factor only using control group data (i.e. individuals who are not treated). 

# STEP 1 (factor model)
model <-'
knowledge =~ test1 +test2+test3+test4
'
latent_model <-sem(model, data = controlgroupdata, std.lv=TRUE)

fullsample$knowledge <- lavPredict(latent_model , data = fullsample
# STEP 2 (regression equation)
lm( knowledge~ treated  , data = fullsample)

This 2-step produce will have the prediction error from the factor score and I understand is not always preferable. 
Is it possible to do this in one step? How can I ask in the model below to estimate the factor loadings of (knowledge =~ test1 +test2+test3+test4) only on control group data?

model_onestep <-'
# Latent factor only on CONTROL group data 
knowledge =~ test1 +test2+test3+test4
# regression equation
knowledge ~ treat
'

impact_evaluation <-sem( model_onestep   , data =  fullsample  , std.lv=TRUE)

Would this be correct?

Many thanks
Dea
